titleText.es: El último sitio donde querría vivir es esa granja que hay al fondo en los diagramas que explican cómo se forman los tornados.
titleText.en: The place I'd least like to live is the farm in the background of those diagrams showing how tornadoes form.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish and English texts are the exact title attributes from the Spanish archive and official xkcd #1472. The source manifest identifies this strip as #1472, but its archived Spanish publication date duplicates #1403; the frozen OCR metadata also incorrectly records #1403 and links to that official page. The raster and official image/metadata unambiguously match #1472, Geography. OCR fused or distorted several hand-lettered map labels; every label here was checked against the Spanish raster.

regions.labelEs: SI PUDIERA ELEGIR DÓNDE VIVIR, ELEGIRÍA EL MAPA DE EJEMPLO DE LOS LIBROS DE GEOGRAFÍA QUE EXPLICA CÓMO SE LLAMAN LAS COSAS.

applications.exampleEs: SI PUDIERA ELEGIR DÓNDE VIVIR, ELEGIRÍA
applications.explanationEn: Si introduces the imagined condition, pudiera supplies its special hypothetical form, and elegiría gives the choice that would follow.
Pudiera changes for the hypothetical situation, while elegir stays in its unchanged -ir dictionary form.
Dónde asks for the unknown place, and vivir stays in its unchanged -ir form.
Dónde keeps its written accent because it asks for an unknown place inside the larger statement.
Dónde introduces an unknown location inside the larger imagined statement, so it keeps its written accent.
Elegiría keeps elegir and adds -ía to express what the speaker would choose.

applications.exampleEs: MAPA DE EJEMPLO DE LOS LIBROS DE GEOGRAFÍA QUE EXPLICA
applications.explanationEn: Mapa is the singular thing being described; que links it to explica, whose singular form matches that map.
Cómo keeps its written accent because it asks about the manner of naming inside the larger statement.
Cómo introduces the unknown naming information in the embedded clause, so it keeps its accent without separate question marks.
Se and llaman form the plural naming verb, while las cosas supplies the plural things whose names are being discussed.

cards.noteEn: Montañas is the plural of montaña and keeps the letter ñ.

cards.promptEs: mi casa · mapa de ejemplo de geografía
cards.questionEn: Why does the speaker want to live inside a textbook-style map?
cards.answerEn: The artificial example map puts nearly every major landform—and the speaker's house—conveniently together.
cards.noteEn: Geography diagrams often compress mountains, rivers, plains, islands, and other features into one implausibly tidy landscape so they can all be labeled. The joke treats that teaching diagram as a desirable real address.
A delta is the landform where a river divides into channels near its mouth. The same word can name the Greek letter delta.

example.es: El río forma un delta junto al mar.
example.en: The river forms a delta by the sea.

cards.noteEn: As a geography noun, estrecho names a narrow channel joining larger bodies of water. As an adjective, it can mean “narrow.”
Río has a written accent to keep the í in a separate spoken syllable.
Bahía has a written accent to keep the í in a separate spoken syllable.

example.es: El puerto está en una bahía.
example.en: The port is in a bay.

cards.noteEn: In geography, a meseta is a broad area of high, relatively flat land.

example.es: La ciudad está sobre una meseta.
example.en: The city is on a plateau.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe an imagined “if…, …would…” situation?
cards.answerEn: Use si followed by a hypothetical past verb form for the condition, and use a “would” form for the result.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls the condition's verb form the imperfect subjunctive. It often ends in -ra or -se, as in tuviera or tuviese. The result uses the conditional, often ending in -ría, as in haría. In this pattern, do not put the conditional directly after si.

example.en: If I had time, I would travel more.

cards.answerEn: I could; if I were able to
cards.noteEn: Pudiera is a hypothetical form of poder, “to be able to.” After si, it presents the ability as imagined rather than real.

example.es: Si pudiera elegir, viajaría en tren.
example.en: If I could choose, I would travel by train.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.
This is the unchanged dictionary form ending in -ir.
Dónde keeps its written accent in an indirect question: the location is being asked about even though the words do not stand alone as a direct question.

example.en: I don't know where Ana lives.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?
How do you say what, how, or where to do something without naming a new person who does it?
cards.answerEn: Use an accented question word, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. This compact pattern is used when the person who would perform the action is already clear from context. The question word keeps its written accent even inside a larger statement: qué hacer, cómo llegar, dónde aparcar.

example.en: I do not know where to park.

cards.questionEn: When “what,” “how,” or “where” introduces unknown information inside a larger sentence, does Spanish keep the written accent?
cards.answerEn: Yes. Keep the accent in qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo, cuál, or quién even when the question is embedded inside a statement.
cards.noteEn: An embedded, or indirect, question reports what is unknown rather than asking it as a separate sentence. It may have no question marks, but the question word still carries its accent. Compare no sé dónde vive, “I don't know where she lives,” with the relative form donde in la casa donde vive, “the house where she lives.”

example.en: I don't know where she lives.

cards.answerEn: I would choose; he or she would choose
cards.noteEn: Elegiría keeps the full dictionary form elegir and adds -ía. This form presents the choice as dependent on an imagined condition or situation.

example.en: I would choose the blue option.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’
Libros is the masculine plural of libro.
Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Explica is the present form of explicar for one person or thing. With a thing as its subject, it says that the thing provides the explanation.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks llamarse, “to be called”
cards.noteEn: Llamarse uses a matching small word: me llamo, te llamas, se llama, nos llamamos, and so on. With he, she, formal you, or one named thing, use se.

cards.questionEn: How do you state what a person or thing is called?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching small pronoun and a form of llamar, then give the name: me llamo, te llamas, se llama, and so on.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is llamarse. The small pronoun changes with the person: me llamo means “I am called,” te llamas is informal “you are called,” and se llama is used for he, she, formal you, or one named thing.

cards.answerEn: they are called; they are named
cards.noteEn: With se, llaman can state what several people or things are called. Llaman itself is the plural present form of llamar.
